word:greek-nt:G0023.explanation: Aganakteo means to be angry or indignant.

word:greek-nt:G0126.explanation: This word means “eternal.” It describes something belonging to unending duration rather than being limited to a temporary period. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice, in Romans 1:20 and Jude 1:6. Its central idea is permanence across time, so it can describe what continually endures. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being described as eternal in each occurrence.

word:greek-nt:G0315.explanation: Anankazō means to force, compel, or constrain. For example, disciples were constrained to get into a boat.

word:greek-nt:G0359.explanation: This word means “departure,” referring to the act of leaving or going away. It is a noun used once in the Greek New Testament, in 2 Timothy 4:6. Its basic sense describes a departure rather than explaining by itself the emotional, spiritual, or situational significance of that departure. The surrounding verse and passage are needed to understand how Paul’s particular use carries meaning there.

word:greek-nt:G0427.explanation: Aneu means without, expressing that something occurs apart from another person or thing.

word:greek-nt:G0485.explanation: This word refers to an argument or dispute—a matter of opposing claims, reasoning, or disagreement between people. It is a noun describing the contention itself rather than the person who argues. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, all in Hebrews and Jude. Its repeated rendering as “dispute” supports the sense of a verbal or reasoned conflict, while “argument” highlights the claim or case being advanced. The surrounding passage determines whether the emphasis is on the disagreement or the argument presented.

word:greek-nt:G0676.explanation: Aprositos means unapproachable, describing light that no human can approach or see.

word:greek-nt:G0742.explanation: Arphaxad is a personal name preserved in the Greek New Testament rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in this corpus, at Luke 3:36. As a proper name, its function is to identify the person being mentioned; the name itself is rendered as “Arphaxad,” not translated into an ordinary descriptive term. This word therefore points to a specific named individual, while the surrounding verse supplies any further significance.

word:greek-nt:G0801.explanation: Asynetos means unintelligent, unwise, or without understanding.

word:greek-nt:G0896.explanation: Baal is the name of a deity to whom people might bow in worship.

word:greek-nt:G0908.explanation: Baptisma means the rite or ceremony of baptism. In one context, John’s baptism is associated with repentance and forgiveness of sins.

word:greek-nt:G0944.explanation: This word means “frogs,” referring to the familiar amphibians. It is a plural noun, so it names more than one frog rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Revelation 16:13. The word’s basic meaning is clear, while its particular significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

word:greek-nt:G1107.explanation: Gnorízō means to make something known or declare it.

word:greek-nt:G1235.explanation: Diagrēgoreō means to wake fully or become thoroughly awake.

word:greek-nt:G1240.explanation: The word means “successor,” referring to someone who follows another in a position, responsibility, or line of succession. It identifies the person who comes after a predecessor rather than the one currently holding the place. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs once, in Acts 24:27. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is the person who follows another. word:greek-nt:G1279.explanation: This word means “to go through,” describing movement from one place or point through an area or route. It is a verb, so it expresses the action of passing along rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, all in five verses, and its uses are found in Luke, Acts, and Romans. The surrounding verse determines what route or area is being traversed.

word:greek-nt:G1297.explanation: Diatagma means a mandate, decree, or edict.

word:greek-nt:G1312.explanation: Diaphthora means decay or corruption. It can also mean destruction.

word:greek-nt:G1451.explanation: Engys means near. It describes physical closeness, as with Bethany near Jerusalem, and can also describe something approaching in time, as summer draws near.

word:greek-nt:G1503.explanation: This word means “to be like” or “to resemble.” It describes likeness between one thing and another, functioning as a verb that says something appears similar or corresponds in some respect. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in James 1. Its basic sense is comparison: one thing is presented as being like something else, rather than as identical to it. The surrounding verse determines exactly what likeness is being expressed in each occurrence.

word:greek-nt:G1680.explanation: Elpis means hope or expectation for what is awaited rather than already seen.

word:greek-nt:G1738.explanation: This word means “just.” It describes what is right or fair rather than wrong or unjust. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, appearing once in Romans and once in Hebrews. Its basic meaning remains focused on justice and rightness; the surrounding verse determines exactly what person, action, or matter is being described. It is rendered “just” in each recorded occurrence.

word:greek-nt:G1819.explanation: This word means “suddenly,” describing something that happens abruptly or without warning. It functions as an adverb, drawing attention to the unexpected timing of an action or change rather than naming the action itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Mark 9:8. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the particular force of that sudden event, but the word itself emphasizes immediacy and unexpectedness.

word:greek-nt:G1820.explanation: Exaporeō means to be in despair.

word:greek-nt:G1855.explanation: Exōthen means outside, from outside, or from without. It can describe the outside of a cup, or something coming from outside a person.

word:greek-nt:G1932.explanation: This word means gentleness: a mild, considerate quality rather than harshness or force. It describes an attitude or manner marked by restraint and kindness. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Acts and 2 Corinthians. Its basic sense points to dealing with others in a gracious, non-severe way, though the surrounding verse determines how that gentleness is expressed. The word’s meaning is therefore clear even when its particular application requires context: it describes a gentle disposition or approach.

word:greek-nt:G1994.explanation: Epistrephō means to turn back, turn toward, or return. It can describe someone physically turning around, and it can also describe people turning back in repentance.

word:greek-nt:G2036.explanation: Legō means to say or speak. It can also introduce a command, as when Jesus said, “You give them something to eat.”

word:greek-nt:G2124.explanation: This word means “reverence”: a serious attitude of respect and honor toward someone regarded as worthy of it. It describes inward regard rather than a specific action, and it can express the proper response of a person before God. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Hebrews, so its normal sense is focused and consistent rather than broad or varied.

word:greek-nt:G2168.explanation: Eucharisteo means to thank or give thanks. It is used when Paul thanked God.

word:greek-nt:G2182.explanation: This word means an inventor: a person who devises or originates something. It identifies someone as a creator of new plans, methods, or things rather than merely someone who repeats what already exists. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Romans 1:30. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains a person who invents or devises something.

word:greek-nt:G2267.explanation: Herodion is a personal name. It refers to a particular person named Herodion, rather than describing an action, quality, object, or general idea. In the Greek New Testament, the name occurs once, in Romans 16:11. Since a personal name identifies someone rather than explains that person’s character or role, its basic meaning is simply the individual’s name. The surrounding verse and passage are needed to understand what is said about Herodion there.

word:greek-nt:G2289.explanation: Thanatoō means to put to death.

word:greek-nt:G2393.explanation: Iaspis means jasper, a precious stone.

word:greek-nt:G2511.explanation: Katharizō means to cleanse or make clean. It can describe a person being made clean, as with a leper, or the outside of a cup being cleaned.

word:greek-nt:G2605.explanation: Katangellō means to declare openly, proclaim, or preach. It is used for proclaiming the resurrection from the dead and God's word.

word:greek-nt:G2649.explanation: Katamartyreo means to give evidence or testify against someone.

word:greek-nt:G2670.explanation: Katapontizo means to sink. It can also mean to be drowned.

word:greek-nt:G2753.explanation: Keleuō means to command, order, direct, or bid someone to act. It is used when people are commanded to sit down and when a chariot is commanded to stand still.

word:greek-nt:G2890.explanation: Quartus is a personal name, referring to a man named Quartus. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Romans 16:23, and is rendered “Quartus.” As a name, it identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. The surrounding verse gives the specific setting in which he is mentioned, but the available word-level information establishes chiefly his name and single occurrence.

word:greek-nt:G2946.explanation: Kylismos means a place of wallowing.

word:greek-nt:G3466.explanation: Mysterion means a mystery or secret that must be revealed. It can also refer to God's previously hidden will when made known.

word:greek-nt:G3563.explanation: Nous means the mind, including the faculty of understanding and reasoning.

word:greek-nt:G3664.explanation: Homoios means like, similar to, or resembling.

word:greek-nt:G3761.explanation: Oude means “neither,” “nor,” “not even,” or “and not.” It can introduce a second negative statement, as in “neither does anyone know the Father.”

word:greek-nt:G3909.explanation: This word means being there or happening to be present at a place. It describes someone who is present, apparently as circumstances bring that person there, rather than emphasizing a deliberate journey or arrival. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 17:17, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central idea remains simple: to be there.

word:greek-nt:G3930.explanation: Parecho means to offer, provide, give, or bring.

word:greek-nt:G3945.explanation: Paromoiazō means to resemble or be like. It is used when scribes and Pharisees are said to be like whitened tombs.

word:greek-nt:G4063.explanation: Peritrechō means to run around or run throughout.

word:greek-nt:G4166.explanation: Poimēn means shepherd, one who watches over a flock. It can also be used figuratively with people pictured as sheep without a shepherd.

word:greek-nt:G4261.explanation: Proballō means to thrust or put something forward. It can also describe something shooting forth, as when it buds.

word:greek-nt:G4328.explanation: Prosdokao means to expect, wait for, or look for someone or something.

word:greek-nt:G4364.explanation: It means “to act as if” or “to pretend”—a verb describing behavior that presents something as though it were so. The word appears once in the Greek New Testament, at Luke 24:28. Its basic sense concerns putting on an appearance or behaving in a way that may not express the person’s actual intention. The surrounding verse context is needed to explain its particular force there.

word:greek-nt:G4531.explanation: Saleuō means to shake. It is used of a reed shaken by the wind and of the powers of the heavens being shaken.

word:greek-nt:G4672.explanation: Solomon is the personal name of David’s son.

word:greek-nt:G4698.explanation: Splanchna means the inward parts or entrails. It can also refer to the heart or to affection.

word:greek-nt:G4737.explanation: Stephanoō means to crown, as someone may be crowned with glory and honor.

word:greek-nt:G4795.explanation: Synkyria means a coincidence, accident, or chance event.

word:greek-nt:G4834.explanation: Sympatheō means to sympathize with or have compassion on someone.

word:greek-nt:G4878.explanation: This word means “helps” or “to help.” It describes coming to another’s aid rather than leaving that person to manage alone. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice, in Luke and Romans, and is translated with forms of “help.” Its basic sense is active assistance: someone gives needed support or joins in meeting a difficulty. The surrounding passage determines who provides the help and what kind of need is being addressed, but the word itself centers on aiding another.

word:greek-nt:G4892.explanation: Synedrion means a council or tribunal, including the Sanhedrin. It can also refer to the meeting place of the Sanhedrin, where people were brought before the council for questioning.

word:greek-nt:G4917.explanation: Synthlaō means to break in pieces, crush, or shatter.

word:greek-nt:G5110.explanation: Tokos means interest or usury on money lent.

word:greek-nt:G5165.explanation: This word means a “bowl,” referring to a vessel or dish used to hold something. It occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, once in Matthew and once in Mark. Both occurrences are recorded in passages numbered Matthew 26:23 and Mark 14:20, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain its particular use there. Its ordinary meaning remains simple and concrete: a bowl or dish that contains something.

word:greek-nt:G5208.explanation: Hylē means wood. It can also refer to a forest.

word:greek-nt:G5301.explanation: This word means “hyssop,” the name of a plant mentioned in the Greek New Testament. It is a noun used for a specific item rather than an action, quality, or person. The word occurs twice in this corpus, once in John and once in Hebrews. Its exact significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning remains the same: hyssop. Both recorded English renderings preserve this meaning directly.

word:greek-nt:G5396.explanation: Phlyareō means to gossip against others. It describes prating against them with malicious words.

word:greek-nt:G5477.explanation: Chanaan is Canaan, the land of Palestine.

word:greek-nt:G5514.explanation: Chloe is a personal name, referring to a woman known to the Corinthian believers. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Corinthians 1:11, in the expression connected with Chloe’s household. The word itself identifies the person rather than describing a spiritual quality, action, or general idea. Since the surrounding verse text is not included here, the broader significance of the report associated with her household belongs to the context of that passage, not to the name itself.

word:greek-nt:G5558.explanation: This word means “to be adorned with gold” or “to gild.” It describes something decorated with gold, functioning as a verb rather than naming the gold itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Revelation. Its basic meaning is therefore clear, while its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and imagery. The word points to outward golden adornment—something made rich or splendid through the use of gold.

word:greek-nt:G5622.explanation: This word means “advantage” or “value”—the benefit, usefulness, or worth something provides. It is a noun that points to what may be gained from a position, privilege, action, or circumstance. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Romans 3:1 and Jude 1:16. Its central idea is practical benefit: whether something offers a real gain or serves a worthwhile purpose. The surrounding passage determines exactly what is being considered valuable or advantageous in each occurrence.

word:greek-nt:G6986.explanation: This word means “if” or “if indeed.” It introduces a condition, presenting something as dependent on another circumstance or possibility. The wording can also add emphasis through the sense “if indeed,” inviting attention to whether the condition truly applies. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in Hebrews. Its precise force in each sentence comes from the surrounding words, but its basic function is to connect a condition with what follows.

word:greek-nt:G7530.explanation: This word means “well done” and expresses approval or praise. It is an exclamation spoken to commend someone for what has been accomplished. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 19:17, so its normal meaning is clear even though its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. The expression is directed toward a person whose action is being affirmed, making it a brief but strong word of commendation.
